notes: CPB kept in slot 4 (MD placement, has popularity) although Maoist; Red Flag CP in 5. Slot 19 (template partner) holds the Burma Workers' Party, whose former cadres serve the Revolutionary Council. U Nu's 1969 exile Parliamentary Democracy Party in 2; Thirty Comrades exiles (Bo Let Ya) as catchy slot 0. Ethnic armies: KNU 1, SSA 14, KIO 20, Rohingya Independence Army 11.

0.name: Yebaw Thongyeik
0.text:
The surviving members of Aung San's wartime Thirty Comrades who broke with Ne Win now form the armed core of U Nu's resistance on the Thai border. Bo Let Ya and Bo Yan Naing, heroes of the independence army, have followed U Nu into exile in 1969 and are raising fighters in camps tolerated by the Thai military.

They are soldiers before democrats: their goal is to topple the Revolutionary Council by force, and they look to Bangkok and, discreetly, Washington for money and arms. Their leverage lies in their names, which still carry weight in the Tatmadaw officer corps.

1.name: Karen National Union
1.text:
The Karen National Union has been fighting the Rangoon government since the insurrection of 1949 for an independent Karen homeland, Kawthoolei. After the splits and surrenders of the 1960s, its president Mahn Ba Zan and the rising commander Bo Mya hold the eastern hill country along the Thai border.

Led largely by Baptist and Anglican Karens, it is fiercely anti-communist and Western in outlook, financing its war by taxing the black-market trade crossing from Thailand. Its leverage lies in a battle-hardened army and the Thai government's interest in a buffer against Burmese and communist forces.

2.name: Parliamentary Democracy Party
2.text:
The Parliamentary Democracy Party was founded in exile in 1969 after former Prime Minister U Nu, released by Ne Win, left Burma and declared himself the country's lawful premier. Run from Bangkok and London with the journalist Edward Law Yone as its organiser, it seeks to rally all opponents of the Revolutionary Council.

It demands a return to the 1947 constitution, a freely elected parliament and the release of political prisoners, and courts Western sympathy and Thai hospitality. U Nu's personal prestige among Buddhists and the old electorate of his Union Party is its greatest asset.

3.name: Bama Soshelit Pati
3.text:
The Burma Socialist Party was the backbone of the Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League and of the Stable AFPFL faction after 1958. Banned in 1964, its leaders U Ba Swe and U Kyaw Nyein spent years in detention and in 1969 urged Ne Win's Internal Unity Advisory Board to restore parliamentary rule.

It stands for democratic socialism, planned development and close ties with Asian socialist parties, rejecting both Moscow and Beijing. Its strength lies in former trade union and peasant organisers, civil servants and the respect its veterans still enjoy among educated Burmans.

4.name: Bama Pyi Kommyunit Pati
4.text:
The Communist Party of Burma, the White Flag communists, has waged armed struggle since 1948. Shattered by Cultural Revolution-style purges in the Pegu Yoma and the killing of chairman Thakin Than Tun in 1968, it is now led by Thakin Zin, while its new Northeast Command under Naw Seng advances from the Chinese border.

It seeks a people's democratic revolution and denounces Ne Win as a fascist. Armed and supplied by Beijing, it is the most serious military threat to the state, drawing on Wa, Kokang and Kachin recruits as much as on Burman peasants.

5.name: Alan Ni Kommyunit Pati
5.text:
The Red Flag Communist Party split from the main communist movement in 1946 under the firebrand Thakin Soe. Reduced to scattered bands, it survives in the jungles of Arakan and the Irrawaddy delta, with its ageing leader still at large and fiercely hostile to all rivals.

It rejects every compromise with the state and denounces both the Soviet Union and China as betrayers of revolution. Its programme is uncompromising agrarian revolution, and its influence rests on Thakin Soe's legend and a few hundred loyal guerrillas rather than any mass base.

6.name: Amyo Batha Thathana
6.text:
Amyo Batha Thathana takes its name from the old Dobama slogan of race, language and religion and gathers nationalist monks, retired Thakins and xenophobic officials who applaud the expulsion of Indian traders and the anti-Chinese riots of 1967. It looks back to Thakin Kodaw Hmaing as its spiritual patron.

It wants Burma sealed against Western culture, foreign capital and missionaries, and Buddhism restored as the soul of the nation. Its leverage lies in the monasteries and in a regime that shares its suspicion of the outside world.

7.name: Military Intelligence Service
7.text:
The Military Intelligence Service is Ne Win's eyes and ears. Grown from the army's field intelligence units, it watches the officer corps, the universities, the monasteries and the former politicians, and runs the informer networks that make dissent in Rangoon dangerous.

It answers to Ne Win alone and has no ideology beyond the survival of the Revolutionary Council. Anti-Western and suspicious of foreigners, it controls arrests, interrogations and travel permits, which gives it quiet power over every ministry and makes it a kingmaker in any succession.

8.name: Mughal Shia Jama Masjid
8.text:
The Moghul Shia Jamah Mosque in central Rangoon is the centre of Burma's small Twelver Shia community, descendants of Persian and Indian merchants who settled under British rule. Its trustees and congregation have been hit hard by the nationalisations and the exodus of Indian traders.

It keeps out of politics, seeks good relations with the authorities and maintains ties with Iran and the Shia centres of India. Its influence is confined to a few thousand worshippers, but its merchant families still have contacts reaching from Rangoon to Bombay and Tehran.

9.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat
9.text:
The Dawoodi Bohra community of Rangoon is a tightly organised Ismaili Shia congregation of Gujarati traders. Like all Bohras it owes absolute obedience to the Da'i al-Mutlaq, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin, who has led the community from Bombay since 1965.

Its religious life is regulated by the clergy down to dress, trade and marriage, and its members avoid open politics. The nationalisation of commerce has driven many families out of Burma, but those who remain form a disciplined, self-financing network that answers to its spiritual head rather than to Rangoon.

10.name: Tablighi Jamaat
10.text:
The Tablighi Jamaat, the Deobandi preaching movement founded in India, has spread through the mosques of Rangoon, Mandalay and Moulmein among Burmese and Indian Muslims. Its worldwide amir is Maulana Inamul Hasan in Delhi, and its local preachers tour Burmese towns in small groups.

It shuns politics entirely and teaches personal piety, prayer and obedience to lawful authority, which makes it acceptable to a suspicious regime. Its strength lies in mosque networks and the steady recruitment of young men at a time when Muslims have no political voice.

11.name: Rohingya Independence Army
11.text:
The Rohingya Independence Army, founded in 1963 as the Rohingya Independence Force by Muhammad Jafar Habib, carries on the armed struggle of the Arakan Mujahids, who surrendered in 1961. It operates in small bands in the Mayu frontier region bordering East Pakistan.

It seeks an autonomous or independent Muslim homeland in northern Arakan and appeals to Pakistan and the wider Islamic world for support. Its fighters are few, but it can draw on the resentment of Rohingya Muslims denied recognition and on sanctuary across the border.

12.name: Burma Muslim Congress
12.text:
The Burma Muslim Congress was founded in 1945 by U Razak, the Muslim minister assassinated with Aung San in 1947, and long served as the Muslim wing of the AFPFL. Dissolved as a political body under the 1964 Law Protecting National Unity, it survives through mosque committees, schools and welfare societies.

It seeks full citizenship and religious freedom for Burmese Muslims within a united, democratic Union, rejecting both separatism and communal politics. Its base is urban Burmese Muslims, and its leverage rests on community networks the regime has not yet broken up.

13.name: Pyidaungsu Tawhlanyay Kaungsi
13.text:
The Union Revolutionary Council has governed Burma by decree since the coup of 2 March 1962. Chaired by General Ne Win, it combines senior officers with a handful of civilian technocrats such as Foreign Minister U Thi Han, and runs the nationalised economy through army-staffed corporations and security and administration committees.

It pursues strict neutrality, accepting neither American nor Soviet patronage, and favours order, central planning and isolation over popular participation. Its power rests on control of every ministry and on the army's monopoly of force.

14.name: Shan State Army
14.text:
The Shan State Army was founded in 1964 under the patronage of Sao Hearn Hkam, the Mahadevi of Yawnghwe and widow of Burma's first president Sao Shwe Thaik, who died in army custody after the 1962 coup. It fights for the rights of the Shan states promised in the 1947 Panglong agreement.

Its leaders, drawn from the old saopha aristocracy and educated Shan youth, demand a true federal union or independence. Its leverage lies in the hills and valleys of Shan State, the opium economy and sympathy across the border in Thailand.

15.name: Ka Kwe Ye
15.text:
The Ka Kwe Ye are government-licensed home guard militias raised in Shan State from 1963 to fight communists and rebels. In return they may use government roads and towns, and they have become the masters of the opium caravans. Lo Hsing Han of the Kokang militia is now the most powerful KKY chief, while his rival Khun Sa was arrested in 1969.

They are loyal only to profit, serving Rangoon against the communists while trading with Thai and Kuomintang buyers. Their leverage lies in private armies, cross-border trade and the regime's dependence on them.

16.name: Burmese Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Burmese Chamber of Commerce was founded in 1919 to represent indigenous Burmese merchants against British, Indian and Chinese competition. Since the nationalisations of 1963 and 1964 its members have lost their firms, shops and import licences, and the chamber survives as a shadow of the business class.

It quietly argues for the return of private enterprise, foreign trade and investment. Its former members and the traders of the black market, which supplies most consumer goods, form a constituency that will welcome any loosening of the socialist economy.

17.name: Burma Forest Department
17.text:
The Burma Forest Department, founded under British rule in the 1850s, manages the teak forests through the Burma Selection System, which allows only mature trees to be felled. Its professional foresters see the forests threatened by insurgency, illegal logging along the borders and pressure to raise timber exports for foreign currency.

It stands for scientific conservancy, wildlife sanctuaries and sustainable yield rather than quick profit. Its influence lies in technical expertise and in the importance of teak, Burma's chief export, to the state's finances.

18.name: Myanma Soshelit Lanzin Pati
18.text:
The Burma Socialist Programme Party was founded by the Revolutionary Council in July 1962 as a cadre party and has been the only legal party since 1964. Chaired by General Ne Win, it is preparing to transform itself from a narrow body of officers and officials into a mass party, guided by the doctrine drafted with ideologue U Chit Hlaing.

Its Burmese Way to Socialism combines Buddhist ethics, Marxist economics and nationalism: state ownership of industry and trade, neutrality between the blocs and self-reliance. Its strength lies in the army and the state machinery it fuses together.

19.name: Bama Alouthama Pati
19.text:
The Burma Workers' Party, heir to the Burma Workers and Peasants Party of the Red Socialists, was the main legal Marxist force of the 1950s and the core of the National United Front. Dissolved in 1964, many of its cadres, including leader Thakin Chit Maung, chose to cooperate with the Revolutionary Council rather than join the insurgents.

It holds that Burma can reach socialism through the existing state, and supports nationalisation and neutrality. Its leverage lies in former cadres placed in economic planning, the press and the official peasants' and workers' councils.

20.name: Wunpawng Mungdan Shanglawt Hpung
20.text:
The Kachin Independence Organisation was founded in 1961 by Zau Seng and his brothers, angered by U Nu's adoption of Buddhism as state religion and the transfer of Kachin villages to China. Its Kachin Independence Army now controls much of the far north, with Zau Seng as chairman.

It demands independence for the Kachin people and rallies a largely Baptist population around ethnic and religious identity. It is anti-communist but clashing with the advancing CPB, and draws its strength from jade mining revenue, tight clan loyalty and rugged terrain.

21.name: Pyu Saw Htee
21.text:
Pyu Saw Htee takes its name from the legendary warrior king and from the village militias U Nu's government raised in the 1950s to fight communist and ethnic rebels. Their veterans now serve in the People's Militia under local army commanders, a rural network of armed Burman nationalists.

They see Burma as a Burman and Buddhist nation threatened by insurgent minorities, Chinese and Indian influence and Western missionaries. Their leverage is local and violent: guns in the villages of the dry zone and the delta, and the patronage of regional commanders.

22.name: Tatmadaw
22.text:
The Tatmadaw, built by Ne Win from the remnants of Aung San's independence army, is the true foundation of the state. Ne Win remains chief of staff, while his trusted deputy San Yu manages the army's daily command and its campaigns against communist and ethnic insurgents.

The officer corps sees itself as the guardian of national unity, the only institution standing between Burma and disintegration. It controls ministries, state corporations and regional administration, and any shift in its loyalties would decide who rules in Rangoon.

23.name: Konbaung Set
23.text:
The House of Konbaung ruled Burma until the British deposed King Thibaw in 1885 and exiled him to India. His grandson Taw Phaya lives quietly in Burma as the head of the royal family, without political role or public following.

Royalist sentiment survives among older Buddhists who associate the crown with the patronage of the Sangha and the old order of Mandalay. Under a revolutionary socialist regime the dynasty has no institutional base, but it remains a symbol of Burmese sovereignty before colonial rule.
